claim: Variant calling is fundamental in bacterial genomics, underpinning the identification of disease transmission clusters, the construction of phylogenetic trees, and antimicrobial resistance detection.
source: Variant calling is fundamental in bacterial genomics, underpinning the identification of disease transmission clusters, the construction of phylogenetic trees, and antimicrobial resistance detection.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Stimson et al., 2019; Sheka et al., 2021; Walker et al., 2022; Bertels et al., 2014) and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Deep learning-based variant callers, particularly Clair3 and DeepVariant, significantly outperform traditional methods on bacterial nanopore sequence data.
source: Our findings reveal that deep learning-based variant callers, particularly Clair3 and DeepVariant, significantly outperform traditional methods and even exceed the accuracy of Illumina sequencing, especially when applied to ONT's super-high accuracy model.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically the F1 scores and performance metrics shown in Figure 2 and Figure 3.

claim: Deep learning-based variant callers exceed the accuracy of Illumina sequencing when applied to ONT's super-high accuracy model.
source: Our findings reveal that deep learning-based variant callers, particularly Clair3 and DeepVariant, significantly outperform traditional methods and even exceed the accuracy of Illumina sequencing, especially when applied to ONT's super-high accuracy model.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing ONT and Illumina variant calling performance shown in Figure 2 and Figure 3.

claim: ONT's superior performance is attributed to its ability to overcome Illumina's errors, which often arise from difficulties in aligning reads in repetitive and variant-dense genomic regions.
source: ONT's superior performance is attributed to its ability to overcome Illumina's errors, which often arise from difficulties in aligning reads in repetitive and variant-dense genomic regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 analyzing variant density and repetitive regions, as well as alignment visualizations in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and 2.

claim: The use of high-performing variant callers with ONT's super-high accuracy data mitigates ONT's traditional errors in homopolymers.
source: Moreover, the use of high-performing variant callers with ONT's super-high accuracy data mitigates ONT's traditional errors in homopolymers.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 analyzing false positive indel calls in homopolymeric regions across different basecalling models.

claim: 10× depth of ONT super-accuracy data can achieve precision and recall comparable to, or better than, full-depth Illumina sequencing.
source: We also investigated the impact of read depth on variant calling, demonstrating that 10× depth of ONT super-accuracy data can achieve precision and recall comparable to, or better than, full-depth Illumina sequencing.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 7 comparing variant calling metrics at different read depths.

claim: Short-read sequencing technologies, such as Illumina, have been the mainstay of variant calling in bacterial genomes over the last 15 years, largely due to their relatively high level of basecalling accuracy.
source: Over the last 15 years, short-read sequencing technologies, such as Illumina, have been the mainstay of variant calling in bacterial genomes, largely due to their relatively high level of basecalling accuracy.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge in the field of genomics.

claim: ONT sequencing has the ability to generate sequencing data in near real time.
source: One of the major advantages of ONT sequencing from an infectious disease's public health perspective is the ability to generate sequencing data in near real time, as well as the portability of the devices, which has enabled researchers to sequence in remote regions, closer to the source of the disease outbreak (Faria et al., 2016; Hoenen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Faria et al., 2016; Hoenen et al., 2016).

claim: ONT devices are portable, enabling researchers to sequence in remote regions closer to the source of disease outbreaks.
source: One of the major advantages of ONT sequencing from an infectious disease's public health perspective is the ability to generate sequencing data in near real time, as well as the portability of the devices, which has enabled researchers to sequence in remote regions, closer to the source of the disease outbreak (Faria et al., 2016; Hoenen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Faria et al., 2016; Hoenen et al., 2016).

claim: Limitations in ONT basecalling accuracy have historically limited its widespread adoption for bacterial genome variant calling.
source: Limitations in ONT basecalling accuracy have historically limited its widespread adoption for bacterial genome variant calling (Delahaye and Nicolas, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Delahaye and Nicolas, 2021).

claim: ONT recently released a new R10.4.1 pore along with a new basecaller with three different accuracy modes (fast, high-accuracy, and super-accuracy).
source: ONT have recently released a new R10.4.1 pore, along with a new basecaller (Oxford Nanopore Technologies, 2023a) with three different accuracy modes (fast, high-accuracy [hac], and super-accuracy [sup]).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Oxford Nanopore Technologies documentation (Oxford Nanopore Technologies, 2023a).

claim: ONT's basecaller has the ability to identify a subset of paired reads for which both strands have been sequenced (duplex), leading to impressive gains in basecalling accuracy.
source: The basecaller also has the ability to identify a subset of paired reads for which both strands have been sequenced (duplex), leading to impressive gains in basecalling accuracy (Sanderson et al., 2023; Sereika et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Sanderson et al., 2023; Sereika et al., 2022).

claim: Previous benchmarking studies for ONT variant calling have focused on human genome variant calling and mostly used older pores without duplex read capability.
source: However, to date, benchmarking studies have focused on human genome variant calling, and have mostly used the older pores, which do not have the ability to identify duplex reads (Olson et al., 2023; Olson et al., 2022; Pei et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Olson et al., 2023; Olson et al., 2022; Pei et al., 2021).

claim: Modern deep learning-based variant callers use models trained on human DNA sequence only.
source: In addition, modern deep learning-based variant callers use models trained on human DNA sequence only, leaving an open question of their generalisability to bacteria (Zheng et al., 2022; Poplin et al., 2018; Ahsan et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Zheng et al., 2022; Poplin et al., 2018; Ahsan et al., 2021).

claim: Human genomes have a very different distribution of k-mers and patterns of DNA modification compared to bacteria.
source: Human genomes have a very different distribution of k-mers (segments of DNA sequence of length k) and patterns of DNA modification, and as such, results from human studies may not directly carry over into bacterial genomics.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge in genomics and is supported by inference from known biological differences.

claim: There is substantial k-mer and DNA modification variation within bacteria.
source: Moreover, there is substantial k-mer and DNA modification variation within bacteria, mandating a broad multi-species approach for evaluation (Tourancheau et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Tourancheau et al., 2021).

claim: Existing benchmarks for bacterial genomes only assess short-read Illumina data.
source: Existing benchmarks for bacterial genomes, while immensely beneficial and thorough, only assess short-read Illumina data (Bush, 2021; Bush et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bush, 2021; Bush et al., 2020).

claim: The study used the same DNA extractions for both Illumina and ONT sequencing to ensure results are not biased by acquisition of new mutations during culture.
source: We used the same DNA extractions for both Illumina and ONT sequencing to ensure our results are not biased by acquisition of new mutations during culture.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: The study developed a novel strategy for generating benchmark variant truthsets by projecting variations from different strains onto gold standard reference genomes.
source: We develop a novel strategy for generating benchmark variant truthsets in which we project variations from different strains onto our gold standard reference genomes in order to create biologically realistic distribution of SNPs and indels.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology developed in the study.

claim: The study analysed 14 samples from different bacterial species spanning a wide range of GC content (30–66%).
source: We analysed 14 samples from different species, spanning a wide range of GC content (30–66%).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Table 1.

claim: Despite variation in SNP counts (2102-57887), the number of indels was consistent across samples.
source: Despite the variation in SNP counts (2102-57887), the number of indels was consistent across samples (see Supplementary file 1b for details).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Table 1 and Supplementary file 1b.

claim: Duplex reads basecalled with the sup model had the highest median read identity of 99.93% (Q32).
source: Duplex reads basecalled with the sup model had the highest median read identity of 99.93% (Q32).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Duplex hac reads had a median read identity of 99.79% (Q27).
source: This was followed by duplex hac (99.79% [Q27]), simplex sup (99.26% [Q21]), simplex hac (98.31% [Q18]), and simplex fast (94.09% [Q12]).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Simplex sup reads had a median read identity of 99.26% (Q21).
source: This was followed by duplex hac (99.79% [Q27]), simplex sup (99.26% [Q21]), simplex hac (98.31% [Q18]), and simplex fast (94.09% [Q12]).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Simplex hac reads had a median read identity of 98.31% (Q18).
source: This was followed by duplex hac (99.79% [Q27]), simplex sup (99.26% [Q21]), simplex hac (98.31% [Q18]), and simplex fast (94.09% [Q12]).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Simplex fast reads had a median read identity of 94.09% (Q12).
source: This was followed by duplex hac (99.79% [Q27]), simplex sup (99.26% [Q21]), simplex hac (98.31% [Q18]), and simplex fast (94.09% [Q12]).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The study benchmarked seven variant callers on ONT sequencing data: BCFtools, Clair3, DeepVariant, FreeBayes, Longshot, Medaka, and NanoCaller.
source: For this study, we benchmarked the performance of seven variant callers on ONT sequencing data: BCFtools (v1.19, Danecek et al., 2021), Clair3 (v1.0.5, Zheng et al., 2022), DeepVariant (v1.6.0, Poplin et al., 2018), FreeBayes (v1.3.7, Garrison, 2012), Longshot (v0.4.5, Edge and Bansal, 2019), Medaka(v1.11.3, Oxford Nanopore Technologies, 2023a; Oxford Nanopore Technologies, 2023c), and NanoCaller (v3.4.1, Ahsan et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design and methods used in the study.

claim: Variants from Illumina data were called using Snippy to act as a performance comparison.
source: In addition, we called variants from each sample's Illumina data using Snippy (v4.6.0, Seemann, 2015) to act as a performance comparison.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design and methods used in the study.

claim: Clair3 and DeepVariant produce the highest F1 scores for both SNPs and indels with both read types.
source: From Figure 2 we see that Clair3 and DeepVariant produce the highest F1 scores for both SNPs and indels with both read types.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The sup basecalling model leads to the highest F1 scores across all variant callers.
source: Unsurprisingly, the sup basecalling model leads to the highest F1 scores across all variant callers, though hac is not much lower.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: SNP F1 scores of 99.99% are obtained from Clair3 and DeepVariant on sup-basecalled data.
source: SNP F1 scores of 99.99% are obtained from Clair3 and DeepVariant on sup-basecalled data.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: For indel calls, Clair3 achieves F1 scores of 99.53% and 99.20% for sup simplex and duplex, respectively.
source: For indel calls, Clair3 achieves F1 scores of 99.53% and 99.20% for sup simplex and duplex, respectively, while DeepVariant scores 99.61% and 99.22%.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: DeepVariant achieves indel F1 scores of 99.61% and 99.22% for sup simplex and duplex, respectively.
source: For indel calls, Clair3 achieves F1 scores of 99.53% and 99.20% for sup simplex and duplex, respectively, while DeepVariant scores 99.61% and 99.22%.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The higher depth of simplex reads likely explains why the best duplex indel F1 scores are slightly lower than simplex.
source: The higher depth of the simplex reads likely explains why the best duplex indel F1 scores are slightly lower than simplex (see How much read depth is enough?).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data and analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Reads basecalled with the fast model are an order of magnitude worse than the hac and sup models.
source: Reads basecalled with the fast model are an order of magnitude worse than the hac and sup models.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Deep learning-based variant callers (Clair3, DeepVariant, Medaka, and NanoCaller) match or surpass Illumina for all variant and read types with hac or sup data.
source: A striking feature of Figure 2 and Figure 3 is the comparison of deep learning-based variant callers (Clair3, DeepVariant, Medaka, and NanoCaller) to Illumina. For all variant and read types with hac or sup data, these deep learning methods match or surpass Illumina, with median best SNP and indel F1 scores of 99.45% and 95.76% for Illumina.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 3.

claim: Illumina has median best SNP and indel F1 scores of 99.45% and 95.76%.
source: For all variant and read types with hac or sup data, these deep learning methods match or surpass Illumina, with median best SNP and indel F1 scores of 99.45% and 95.76% for Illumina.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Traditional variant callers (Longshot, BCFtools, and FreeBayes) match or slightly exceed Illumina for SNP calls with hac and sup data.
source: Traditional variant callers (Longshot, BCFtools, and FreeBayes) match or slightly exceed Illumina for SNP calls with hac and sup data.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: FreeBayes matches Illumina for indel calls.
source: FreeBayes matches Illumina for indel calls, but BCFtools shows reduced indel accuracy across all models and read types.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: BCFtools shows reduced indel accuracy across all models and read types.
source: FreeBayes matches Illumina for indel calls, but BCFtools shows reduced indel accuracy across all models and read types.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Fast model ONT data has a lower F1 score than Illumina, only achieving parity in the best case for SNPs.
source: Fast model ONT data has a lower F1 score than Illumina, only achieving parity in the best case for SNPs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Illumina's lower F1 score is mainly due to recall rather than precision.
source: Figure 2—figure supplement 1 shows that Illumina's lower F1 score is mainly due to recall rather than precision (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Variant density and repetitive regions account for many false negatives in Illumina data, lowering recall.
source: Figure 4 shows that variant density and repetitive regions account for many false negatives, lowering recall.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Illumina false negatives show a bimodal distribution of variant density with a second peak at 20 variants per 100 bp.
source: Figure 4a reveals a bimodal distribution of variant density for Illumina FNs, with a second peak at 20 variants per 100 bp, unlike the distribution for TP and FP calls.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Clair3 shows no bimodal distribution and few missed or false calls at high variant density.
source: In contrast, Clair3, a top-performing ONT variant caller, shows no bimodal distribution and few missed or false calls at this density (Figure 4b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Illumina reads struggle to align in variant-dense regions, whereas ONT reads can.
source: Illumina reads struggle to align in variant-dense regions, whereas ONT reads can (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), as 20 variants per 100 bp represents a larger portion of an Illumina read than an ONT read.
evidence: This claim is supported by the alignment visualization shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and inference from read length differences.

claim: Illumina's F1 score increases from 99.3% to 99.7% when repetitive regions are masked.
source: This is further quantified by the increase in Illumina's F1 score when repetitive regions are masked (Figure 4c), rising from 99.3% to 99.7%.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Clair3 100× simplex sup data shows only a 0.003% increase in F1 score when repetitive regions are masked.
source: In contrast, Clair3 100× simplex sup data shows only a 0.003% increase.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Reads basecalled with the fast model often miscalculate homopolymer lengths by 1 or 2 bp.
source: When analysing Clair3, the best-performing ONT caller, we found that reads basecalled with the fast model often miscalculate homopolymer lengths by 1 or 2 bp (Figure 5), though there is an equal number of non-homopolymeric false indel calls.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The sup model significantly reduced false indel calls, matching Illumina's error profile.
source: In contrast, the sup model significantly reduced false indel calls, matching Illumina's error profile.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Of the eight false indel calls by Clair3 on sup data, five were homopolymers and three occurred within one or two bases of another insertion with a similar sequence.
source: Of the eight false indel calls by Clair3 on sup data, five were homopolymers and three occurred within one or two bases of another insertion with a similar sequence.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data analysis of false indel calls.

claim: The hac model improved over the fast model but still produced notable false indel calls, mainly miscalculating homopolymers by 1 bp.
source: The hac model improved over the fast model but still produced notable false indel calls, mainly miscalculating homopolymers by 1 bp.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: DeepVariant showed a similar error profile to Clair3, with 8/11 false indels being homopolymers.
source: DeepVariant showed a similar error profile to Clair3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), with 8/11 false indels being homopolymers.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: BCFtools exhibited a persistent bias for homopolymeric indel errors, even with sup model reads.
source: BCFtools (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) exhibited a persistent bias for homopolymeric indel errors, even with sup model reads.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The sup basecaller reduces bias, but deep learning methods like Clair3 and DeepVariant further mitigate it by training models to account for systematic issues.
source: This indicates that while the sup basecaller reduces bias, deep learning methods like Clair3 and DeepVariant further mitigate it by training models to account for these systematic issues.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data comparing different basecalling models and variant callers.

claim: Clair3 or DeepVariant on 10× ONT sup simplex data provides F1 scores consistent with, or better than, full-depth Illumina for both SNPs and indels.
source: Remarkably, Clair3 or DeepVariant on 10× ONT sup simplex data provides F1 scores consistent with, or better than, full-depth Illumina for both SNPs and indels (see Supplementary file 1a for Illumina read depths).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 7.

claim: 10× duplex hac or sup reads provide F1 scores consistent with, or better than, full-depth Illumina for both SNPs and indels.
source: The same is true for duplex hac or sup reads.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 7.

claim: With 5× of ONT read depth the F1 score is lower than Illumina for almost all variant caller and basecalling models.
source: With 5× of ONT read depth the F1 score is lower than Illumina for almost all variant caller and basecalling models.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 7.

claim: BCFtools produces SNP F1 scores on par with Illumina on duplex sup reads at 5× depth.
source: However, BCFtools surprisingly produces SNP F1 scores on par with Illumina on duplex sup reads.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6.

claim: SNP precision remains above Illumina at 5× depth with duplex reads for all methods except NanoCaller, and calls from Clair3 and DeepVariant simplex sup data.
source: Despite the inferior F1 scores across the board at 5×, SNP precision remains above Illumina with duplex reads for all methods except NanoCaller, and calls from Clair3 and DeepVariant simplex sup data.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6.

claim: DeepVariant was the slowest variant caller with a median runtime of 5.7 s/Mbp.
source: DeepVariant was the slowest (median 5.7 s/Mbp) and most memory-intensive (median 8 GB), with a runtime of 38 min for a 4 Mbp genome at 100× depth.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 8.

claim: DeepVariant was the most memory-intensive variant caller with a median of 8 GB.
source: DeepVariant was the slowest (median 5.7 s/Mbp) and most memory-intensive (median 8 GB), with a runtime of 38 min for a 4 Mbp genome at 100× depth.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 8.

claim: FreeBayes had the largest runtime variation, with a maximum of 597 s/Mbp, equating to 2.75 days for a 4 Mbp genome at 100× depth.
source: FreeBayes had the largest runtime variation, with a maximum of 597 s/Mbp, equating to 2.75 days for the same genome.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Basecalling with a single GPU using the super-accuracy model required a median runtime of 0.77 s/Mbp, or just over 5 min for a 4 Mbp genome at 100× depth.
source: In contrast, basecalling with a single GPU using the super-accuracy model required a median runtime of 0.77 s/Mbp, or just over 5 min for a 4 Mbp genome at 100× depth.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Clair3 had a median memory usage of 1.6 GB and a runtime of 0.86 s/Mbp (<6 min for a 4 Mbp 100× genome).
source: Clair3 had a median memory usage of 1.6 GB and a runtime of 0.86 s/Mbp (<6 min for a 4 Mbp 100× genome).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Read accuracies greater than 99.0% (Q20) and 99.9% (Q30) were observed for simplex and duplex reads, respectively.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Sanderson et al., 2024; Sanderson et al., 2023; Sereika et al., 2022), we observed read accuracies greater than 99.0% (Q20) and 99.9% (Q30) for simplex and duplex reads, respectively (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1 and citations to previous studies (Sanderson et al., 2024; Sanderson et al., 2023; Sereika et al., 2022).

claim: Recent improvements in ONT read accuracy and deep learning-based variant callers have mitigated homopolymer-induced FP indel calls.
source: However, we found recent improvements in ONT read accuracy and deep learning-based variant callers have mitigated homopolymer-induced FP indel calls, previously a major systematic issue with ONT data (Delahaye and Nicolas, 2021; Sereika et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5 and citations to previous studies (Delahaye and Nicolas, 2021; Sereika et al., 2022).

claim: High accuracy is achievable at reduced read depths of 10×, especially with super-accuracy basecalling models and deep learning algorithms.
source: Our results show that high accuracy is achievable at reduced read depths of 10×, especially with super-accuracy basecalling models and deep learning algorithms.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 7.

claim: 10× super-accuracy simplex data can match or exceed Illumina accuracy.
source: This is significant for resource-limited projects, as 10× super-accuracy simplex data can match or exceed Illumina accuracy.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 7.

claim: For optimal clinical and public health applications, a minimum of 25× depth is recommended.
source: For optimal clinical and public health applications, we recommend a minimum of 25× depth.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 7.

claim: 5× depth with duplex super-accuracy ONT data achieved SNP accuracy comparable to Illumina.
source: Notably, 5× depth with duplex super-accuracy ONT data achieved SNP accuracy comparable to Illumina.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The study only assessed small variants and ignored structural variants.
source: The first is that we only assess small variants and ignored structural variants.
evidence: This claim describes a limitation of the study.

claim: The study did not use a diverse range of ANI values for selecting the variant donor genomes when generating the truthset.
source: The second limitation is not using a diverse range of ANI values for selecting the variant donor genomes when generating the truthset.
evidence: This claim describes a limitation of the study.

claim: Illumina sequencing was performed on different models: three samples on the NextSeq 500 and the rest on the NextSeq 2000.
source: The third limitation is that Illumina sequencing was performed on different models: three samples on the NextSeq 500 and the rest on the NextSeq 2000.
evidence: This claim describes a limitation of the study.

claim: Differences in error rates exist between Illumina instruments, but no specific assessment has been made between NextSeq 500 and NextSeq 2000 models.
source: While differences in error rates exist between Illumina instruments, no specific assessment has been made between these NextSeq models (Stoler and Nekrutenko, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Stoler and Nekrutenko, 2021).

claim: The absolute differences in error rates between NextSeq models are minor and unlikely to impact the study significantly.
source: However, the absolute differences in error rates are minor and unlikely to impact our study significantly.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from known characteristics of Illumina sequencing platforms.

claim: Ground truth reference assemblies were generated for each sample using ONT and Illumina reads.
source: Ground truth reference assemblies were generated for each sample using ONT and Illumina reads (see Genome assembly).
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The pseudo-real approach for generating variant truthsets has the advantage of a simulation with the added benefit of the variants being real differences between two genomes.
source: This approach has the advantage of a simulation, in that we can be certain of the truthset of variants, but with the added benefit of the variants being real differences between two genomes.
evidence: This claim describes the rationale for the methodology used in the study.

claim: For each sample, a donor genome with average nucleotide identity (ANI) closest to 99.5% was selected.
source: For each sample, we selected a donor genome with average nucleotide identity (ANI; a measure of similarity between two genomes) closest to 99.5% (see Truthset and reference generation).
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Variants between the sample and donor were identified using minimap2 and mummer.
source: We identified all variants between the sample and donor using minimap2 (Li, 2018) and mummer (Marçais et al., 2018), intersected the variant sets, and removed overlaps and indels longer than 50 bp.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The variant truthset was applied to the sample's reference to create a mutated reference.
source: This variant truthset was then applied to the sample's reference to create a mutated reference, ensuring no complications from large structural differences.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Raw ONT data were basecalled with Dorado using the v4.3.0 models fast, hac, and sup.
source: Raw ONT data were basecalled with Dorado (v0.5.0, Oxford Nanopore Technologies, 2023a) using the v4.3.0 models fast (dna_r10.4.1_e8.2_400bps_fast@v4.3.0), hac (dna_r10.4.1_e8.2_400bps_hac@v4.3.0), and sup (dna_r10.4.1_e8.2_400bps_sup@v4.3.0).
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Duplex reads were generated using the duplex subcommand of Dorado with hac and sup models.
source: Duplex reads were additionally generated using the duplex subcommand of Dorado with hac and sup models (fast is not compatible with duplex).
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Reads shorter than 1000bp or with a quality score below 10 were removed.
source: Reads shorter than 1000bp or with a quality score below 10 were removed with SeqKit (v2.6.1 Shen et al., 2016) and each readset was randomly subsampled to a maximum mean read depth of 100x with Rasusa (v0.8.0 Hall, 2022).
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Each readset was randomly subsampled to a maximum mean read depth of 100x.
source: Reads shorter than 1000bp or with a quality score below 10 were removed with SeqKit (v2.6.1 Shen et al., 2016) and each readset was randomly subsampled to a maximum mean read depth of 100x with Rasusa (v0.8.0 Hall, 2022).
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Illumina reads were preprocessed with fastp to remove adapter sequences, trim low-quality bases, and remove duplicate reads and reads shorter than 30bp.
source: Illumina reads were preprocessed with fastp (v0.23.4, Chen et al., 2018) to remove adapter sequences, trim low-quality bases from the ends of the reads, and remove duplicate reads and reads shorter than 30bp.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: ONT reads were aligned to the mutated reference with minimap2 using options --cs --MD -aLx map-ont.
source: ONT reads were aligned to the mutated reference with minimap2 using options --cs --MD -aLx map-ont and output to a BAM alignment file.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Variant calls were assessed against the truthset using vcfdist, classifying each variant as true positive (TP), false positive (FP), or false negative (FN).
source: Variant calls were assessed against the truthset using vcfdist (v2.3.3, Dunn and Narayanasamy, 2023), classifying each variant as true positive (TP), false positive (FP), or false negative (FN).
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Precision, recall, and the F1 score were calculated for SNPs and indels at each VCF quality score increment.
source: Precision, recall, and the F1 score were calculated for SNPs and indels at each VCF quality score increment.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall.
source: The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall and acts as a good metric for overall evaluation.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge in statistics and machine learning.

claim: Due to the right-angle-like shape of the Clair3 and DeepVariant precision-recall curves, filtering based on low-value variant quality improves precision considerably without losing much recall.
source: Due to the right-angle-like shape of the Clair3 and DeepVariant curves, filtering based on low-value variant quality improves precision considerably for variant calls, without losing much recall.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The best Clair3 and DeepVariant F1 scores are obtained with no quality filtering on sup data, except for indels from duplex data where a quality filter of 4 provides the best F1.
source: The best Clair3 and DeepVariant F1 scores are obtained with no quality filtering on sup data, except for indels from duplex data where a quality filter of 4 provides the best F1.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Variant density is defined as the number of variants (missed or called) in a 100 bp window around each call.
source: We define variant density as the number of variants (missed or called) in a 100 bp window around each call.
evidence: This claim describes a definition used in the study.

claim: 20 variants per 100 bp represents a larger portion of an Illumina read than an ONT read.
source: Illumina reads struggle to align in variant-dense regions, whereas ONT reads can (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), as 20 variants per 100 bp represents a larger portion of an Illumina read than an ONT read.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the known read lengths of Illumina and ONT sequencing technologies.

claim: Illumina reads struggle more with alignment in repetitive regions compared to ONT reads due to their shorter length.
source: Due to their shorter length, Illumina reads struggle more with alignment in these regions compared to ONT reads (Treangen and Salzberg, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Treangen and Salzberg, 2011) and inference from read length differences.

claim: Indels have traditionally been a systematic weakness for ONT sequencing data, primarily driven by variability in the length of homopolymeric regions as determined by basecallers.
source: Indels have traditionally been a systematic weakness for ONT sequencing data, primarily driven by variability in the length of homopolymeric regions as determined by basecallers (Delahaye and Nicolas, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Delahaye and Nicolas, 2021).

claim: The study subsampled each ONT read set to average depths of 5×, 10×, 25×, 50×, and 100× to investigate the required ONT read depth.
source: We subsampled each ONT read set with rasusa (v0.8.0, Hall, 2022) to average depths of 5×, 10×, 25×, 50×, and 100× and called variants with these reduced sets.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Due to limited duplex depth, 50× was the maximum used for duplex reads, while 100× was used for simplex reads.
source: Due to limited duplex depth, 50× was the maximum used for duplex reads, while 100× was used for simplex reads.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Precision and recall decrease as read depth is reduced, notably below 25×.
source: Precision and recall decrease as read depth is reduced, notably below 25×.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 7.

claim: Most variant calling methods run in less than 40 min.
source: Most methods, however, run in less than 40 min, with Clair3 having a median runtime of about 6 minutes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 8.

claim: All variant calling methods use less than 8 GB of memory, making them compatible with most laptops.
source: All methods use less than 8 GB of memory, making them compatible with most laptops.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Basecalling is generally faster than variant calling, assuming GPU access.
source: Basecalling is generally faster than variant calling, assuming GPU access, which is likely considered when acquiring ONT-related equipment.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Previous work from Bush et al. found that the diversity threshold for selecting reference genomes is one of the main differentiating factors in accuracy when calling variants from Illumina data.
source: Previous work from Bush et al. examined different diversity thresholds for selecting reference genomes when calling variants from Illumina data, and found it to be one of the main differentiating factors in accuracy (Bush et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Bush et al., 2020).

claim: The study's results mirror previous findings showing the reduction in Illumina accuracy as the variant density increases.
source: Our results mirror this to an extent, showing the reduction in Illumina accuracy as the variant density increases, though it would be interesting to determine whether the divergence in reference genomes has an affect on ONT variant calling accuracy.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4 and inference from previous studies.

claim: Bacterial isolates were streaked onto agar plates and grown overnight at 37°C.
source: Bacterial isolates were streaked onto agar plates and grown overnight at 37°C.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: M. tuberculosis, S. pyogenes, and S. dysgalactiae subsp. equisimilis were grown in liquid media of 7H9 or TSB with shaking until reaching high cell density (OD ∼ 1).
source: M. tuberculosis, S. pyogenes, and S. dysgalactiae subsp. equisimilis were grown in liquid media of 7H9 or TSB with shaking until reaching high cell density (OD ∼ 1; see Appendix 1 for Streptococcus sample selection).
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: DNA extraction was performed by sodium acetate precipitation and further Ampure XP bead purification or either Beckman Coulter GenFind V2 or QIAGEN Blood and Tissue DNEasy kit.
source: DNA extraction was performed by sodium acetate precipitation and further Ampure XP bead purification (Beckman Coulter) or either Beckman Coulter GenFind V2 (A41497) or QIAGEN Blood and Tissue DNEasy kit (69506).
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Illumina library preparation was performed using Illumina DNA prep using quarter reagents and Illumina DNA/RNA UD Indexes.
source: Illumina library preparation was performed using Illumina DNA prep (20060059) using quarter reagents and Illumina DNA/RNA UD Indexes.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Short-read whole-genome sequencing was performed on an Illumina NextSeq 500 for three samples and a NextSeq 2000 for all other samples, with a 150 bp PE kit.
source: Short-read whole-genome sequencing was performed on an Illumina NextSeq 500 for the M. tuberculosis (AMtb_1__202402), S. pyogenes (RDH275__202311), and S. dysgalactiae (MMC234__202311) samples and a NextSeq 2000 for all other samples, with a 150 bp PE kit.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: ONT library preparation was performed using either Rapid Barcoding Kit V14 or Native Barcoding Kit V14.
source: ONT library preparation was performed using either Rapid Barcoding Kit V14 (SQK-RBK114.96) or Native Barcoding Kit V14 (SQK-NBD114.96).
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Long-read whole-genome sequencing was performed on a MinION Mk1b or GridION using R10.4.1 MinION flow cells.
source: Long-read whole-genome sequencing was performed on a MinION Mk1b or GridION using R10.4.1 MinION flow cells (FLO-MIN114).
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: All basecalling runs were performed on an Nvidia A100 GPU to ensure consistency.
source: All runs were basecalled on an Nvidia A100 GPU to ensure consistency.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Ground truth assemblies were generated using the Extra-thorough assembly instructions in Trycycler's documentation.
source: We performed 24 separate assemblies using the Extra-thorough assembly instructions in Trycycler's (v0.5.4, Wick et al., 2021) documentation.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Assemblies were combined into a single consensus assembly with Trycycler and Illumina reads were used to polish that assembly using Polypolish and Pypolca.
source: Assemblies were combined into a single consensus assembly with Trycycler and Illumina reads were used to polish that assembly using Polypolish (v0.6.0; default settings, Wick and Holt, 2022) and Pypolca (v0.3.1, Bouras et al., 2024; Zimin and Salzberg, 2020) with --careful.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Manual curation and investigation of all polishing changes was made as per Wick et al., 2023.
source: Manual curation and investigation of all polishing changes was made as per Wick et al., 2023 (e.g. for very long homopolymers, the correct length was chosen as per Illumina reads support).
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: To select the variant-donor genome, all RefSeq assemblies for that species were downloaded (up to a maximum of 10,000) using genome_updater.
source: To select the variant-donor genome for a given sample, we downloaded all RefSeq assemblies for that species (up to a maximum of 10,000) using genome_updater (v0.6.3, Piro, 2023).
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: ANI was calculated between each downloaded genome and the sample reference using skani.
source: ANI was calculated between each downloaded genome and the sample reference using skani (v0.2.1, Shaw and Yu, 2023).
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Genomes with CheckM completeness less than 98% and contamination greater than 5% were excluded.
source: In addition, we excluded any genomes with CheckM (Parks et al., 2015) completeness less than 98% and contamination greater than 5%.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The genome with the ANI closest to 99.50% was selected as the variant-donor genome.
source: We then selected the genome with the ANI closest to 99.50%.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Variants between the reference and donor genomes were identified using both minimap2 and mummer.
source: We then identified variants between the reference and donor genomes using both minimap2 (v2.26, Li, 2018) and mummer (v4.0.0rc1, Marçais et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The intersection of the variants identified by minimap2 and mummer was taken into a single variant call file (VCF).
source: We took the intersection of the variants identified by minimap2 and mummer into a single variant call file (VCF) and used BCFtools (v1.19, Danecek et al., 2021) to decompose multi-nucleotide polymorphisms (MNPs) into SNPs, left-align and normalise indels, remove duplicate and overlapping variants, and exclude any indel longer than 50 bp.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: BCFtools was used to decompose multi-nucleotide polymorphisms (MNPs) into SNPs, left-align and normalise indels, remove duplicate and overlapping variants, and exclude any indel longer than 50 bp.
source: We took the intersection of the variants identified by minimap2 and mummer into a single variant call file (VCF) and used BCFtools (v1.19, Danecek et al., 2021) to decompose multi-nucleotide polymorphisms (MNPs) into SNPs, left-align and normalise indels, remove duplicate and overlapping variants, and exclude any indel longer than 50 bp.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: BCFtools' consensus subcommand was used to apply the truthset of variants to the sample reference, producing a mutated reference.
source: BCFtools' consensus subcommand was used to apply the truthset of variants to the sample reference, thus producing a mutated reference.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: For Clair3, the pretrained models for Dorado model v4.3.0 provided by ONT were used.
source: For Clair3, the pretrained models for Dorado model v4.3.0 provided by ONT were used (Oxford Nanopore Technologies, 2023c).
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: For Clair3, the hac model was used with fast-basecalled reads because no fast model is available.
source: However, as no fast model is available, we used the hac model with the fast-basecalled reads.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The pretrained model option --model_type ONT_R104 was used with DeepVariant.
source: The pretrained model option --model_type ONT_R104 was used with DeepVariant, and the default model was used for NanoCaller.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: For Medaka, the provided v4.3.0 sup and hac models were used, with the hac model being used for fast data as no fast model is available.
source: For Medaka, the provided v4.3.0 sup and hac models were used, with the hac model being used for fast data as no fast model is available.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Snippy performs alignment of reads with BWA-MEM and calls variants with FreeBayes.
source: Snippy performs alignment of reads with BWA-MEM (Li, 2013) and calls variants with FreeBayes.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology of the Snippy tool.

claim: VCFs were filtered to remove overlapping variants, make heterozygous calls homozygous for the allele with the most depth, normalise and left-align indels, break MNPs into SNPs, and remove indels longer than 50 bp.
source: VCFs were then filtered to remove overlapping variants, make heterozygous calls homozygous for the allele with the most depth, normalise and left-align indels, break MNPs into SNPs, and remove indels longer than 50 bp, all with BCFtools.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Filtered VCFs were assessed with vcfdist using the truth VCFs and mutated references.
source: Filtered VCFs were assessed with vcfdist (v2.3.3, Dunn and Narayanasamy, 2023) using the truth VCFs and mutated references from Truthset and reference generation.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Partial credit was disabled in vcfdist with --credit-threshold 1.0.
source: We disabled partial credit with --credit-threshold 1.0 and set the maximum variant quality threshold (-mx) to the maximum in the VCF being assessed.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: To identify repetitive regions, nucmer was used with --maxmatch --nosimplify to align the reference against itself and retain non-unique alignments.
source: To identify repetitive regions in the mutated reference, we used the following mummer utilities. nucmer --maxmatch --nosimplify to align the reference against itself and retain non-unique alignments.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: show-coords -rTH -I 60 was used to obtain the coordinates for all alignments with an identity of 60% or greater.
source: We then passed the output into show-coords -rTH -I 60 to obtain the coordinates for all alignments with an identity of 60% or greater.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Alignments where the start and end coordinates do not match are considered as repeats.
source: Alignments where the start and end coordinates of the alignment do not match are considered as repeats and these are output in the BED format, with intervals being merged with BEDtools (Quinlan and Hall, 2010).
evidence: This claim describes the methodology used in the study.
